title: Web Crawler
vague_prompt: Design a web crawler for a search engine.
hidden_guidance: Crawl 1 billion pages per month, about 400 pages per second on average
Politeness: at most one request per second to one host
Re-crawl popular pages every 24 hours and the rest every 30 days
The crawler must obey robots.txt for every host and the site terms of record
About 30 percent of fetched pages are near-duplicates of another page
The frontier must survive a worker crash without losing a queued URL
known_patterns: Frontier queue with priority by freshness and page importance
Per host politeness delay and a host level queue
robots.txt fetch and cache per host
Dedup with a Bloom filter on the URL and a content hash on the page
DNS cache to cut lookup cost
Distributed worker pool with a durable frontier store
common_misses: Crawler traps and infinite URL spaces
robots.txt cache expiry and crawl-delay parsing
One slow host blocking a shared queue
Near-duplicate detection with a simhash or shingle set
Re-crawl schedule and URL freshness score

interviewer_brief.gist: A polite queue with a dedup problem. About 400 pages per second on average, and every host allows only one request per second, so the crawler is mostly a scheduler. The other half is noticing that about a third of what it fetched, it already had.

1: About 1 billion pages per month, about 400 pages per second on average
Politeness caps one request per second per host
Popular pages re-crawl every 24 hours, the rest every 30 days
A strong candidate converts the monthly budget into a rate and asks about politeness rules instead of inventing them.
2: A frontier of URLs with priority and schedule, workers that fetch, and a store that keeps pages
The scheduler holds per-host queues so politeness is per host, not per worker
Sketch the loop: pull from frontier, check robots, fetch, extract links, push new URLs
A strong candidate draws the frontier as the heart of the system.
3: robots.txt fetched and cached per host, obeyed for every request
A URL seen-set and content hashes dedupe pages before storage
The page store records fetch time per URL, so schedules re-crawl on their own clocks
A strong candidate caches robots per host and records what was allowed.
4: The politeness ceiling is the bottleneck: 400 pages per second needs at least 386 hosts in flight
Slow or large hosts stall a worker; per-host queues stop one bad host from blocking the fleet
About 30 percent of fetches are near-duplicates, so dedup runs before parsing and storage, not after
A strong candidate sizes the seen-set and the hash store for billions of URLs.
5: The frontier persists: a worker crash loses no queued URL, so the queue is durable or journaled
Re-crawl schedules ride the page record: fetched at, next fetch at
Rate limits and retries per host keep the crawl inside each site's terms
A strong candidate treats crash recovery as a first class requirement, not an afterthought.

anchors.1: Hearing the rate: the candidate converts 1 billion pages per month into about 400 pages per second
anchors.2: Hearing the politeness: the candidate caps one request per second per host and builds per-host queues
anchors.3: Hearing the schedule: the candidate re-crawls popular pages every 24 hours and the rest every 30 days
anchors.4: Hearing the rules: the candidate fetches and obeys robots.txt per host and keeps site terms
anchors.5: Hearing the duplicates: the candidate expects about 30 percent near-duplicates and dedupes by content hash
anchors.6: Hearing the durability: the candidate guarantees a crashed worker loses no queued URL

probes.q: Politeness allows one request per second per host. What does that imply about how many hosts you must crawl in parallel?
Walk me through one URL's life from discovery to stored page.
A site forbids crawling two of its ten sections. Where is that enforced, and where is it remembered?
One host serves one page every eight seconds under load. What does your crawler do to it, and to itself?
About 30 percent of fetches turn out to be duplicates. Where in the pipeline do you catch them, and what do you skip?
A worker dies holding 50 queued URLs in memory. Show me what gets lost, if anything.
